questions.stem: Customary international law is formed when there is:
options: a written agreement signed and ratified by the leaders of at least two neighbouring states
a majority vote in the UN General Assembly in favour of a new legal rule
a judgment of the International Court of Justice that creates a new rule
widespread and consistent state practice, accepted by states as legally required
questions.explanation: Custom needs two elements: consistent state practice and opinio juris, the belief that the practice is legally required. A written agreement between states is a treaty, and General Assembly votes and court judgments are not in themselves the way custom forms.

questions.stem: A state argues that it is bound by a customary rule only because it believes the practice is obligatory, not merely habitual. Which element of customary law is this?
options: Ratification
Pacta sunt servanda
Jus soli
Opinio juris
questions.explanation: Opinio juris is the sense of legal obligation that turns a habit of states into binding custom. Pacta sunt servanda is the principle that treaties must be performed, and ratification is how a state consents to a treaty.

questions.stem: Which document lists the sources of international law that the International Court of Justice applies?
options: Article 38 of the Statute of the International Court of Justice
Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
Section 51 of the Commonwealth of Australia Constitution
The preamble to the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations 1961
questions.explanation: Article 38 of the ICJ Statute directs the court to apply treaties, international custom and general principles of law, with judicial decisions and the writings of highly qualified experts as subsidiary means. The UDHR and Australian Constitution do not set out the sources of international law.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of soft law in the international legal system?
options: A rule of customary law that states follow because they believe it is legally required of them
A judgment of the International Court of Justice in a dispute between two consenting states
A declaration adopted by the UN General Assembly that sets standards but does not bind states
A treaty that has been ratified by a state and has entered into force for that particular state
questions.explanation: Soft law refers to non-binding instruments, such as declarations and guidelines, that still influence state behaviour and can later become binding. A ratified treaty, an established custom and an ICJ judgment for the parties are all binding.

questions.stem: Why are rules such as the prohibition of genocide described as jus cogens (peremptory norms)?
options: They are rules of domestic law that each state has agreed to apply in its own national courts
They are non-binding guidelines that states may choose to follow when it suits their interests
They bind every state and no treaty may override them, whether or not a state has consented
They bind only the states that have ratified the treaty in which the particular rule is written
questions.explanation: Jus cogens norms are accepted by the international community as rules from which no derogation is permitted, and a treaty that conflicts with one is void under Article 53 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties. They bind all states regardless of consent, unlike ordinary treaty rules.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (1969)?
options: It lists the human rights that every state must protect within its own borders
It sets out the rules for how treaties between states are made, interpreted and ended
It sets out the rights and immunities of diplomats working in another state's territory
It creates the International Court of Justice and sets out how its judges are elected
questions.explanation: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties is often called the treaty on treaties: it covers how treaties are concluded, interpreted, amended and terminated. Diplomatic immunities are dealt with by the separate Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations of 1961.

questions.stem: What is the difference between signing a treaty and ratifying it?
options: Signing makes the treaty binding at once, while ratification is a ceremony held years later to celebrate it
Signing is done by parliament, while ratification is done by the courts after they have checked the text
Signing applies to bilateral treaties, while ratification applies only to treaties with many parties
Signing shows support and intention, while ratification is the act by which a state agrees to be bound
questions.explanation: Signature usually indicates a state's intention to become a party, while ratification expresses its consent to be bound. In Australia both are executive acts; parliament's role is to scrutinise the treaty and pass any laws needed to implement it.

questions.stem: A state signs a treaty but has not yet ratified it. Under Article 18 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, it must:
options: ratify the treaty within one year or pay compensation to the other parties
pass domestic laws implementing the treaty before it is allowed to ratify it
refrain from acts that would defeat the object and purpose of the treaty
carry out every obligation in the treaty exactly as a ratifying state would
questions.explanation: Signature alone does not bind a state to perform the treaty, but Article 18 obliges it not to defeat the treaty's object and purpose until it makes clear it will not become a party. There is no time limit for ratification and no compensation rule.

questions.stem: The principle of pacta sunt servanda means that:
options: the most recent treaty always overrides every earlier rule of customary international law
every treaty in force binds the parties and must be performed by them in good faith
a state may withdraw from any treaty at any time without notice to the other parties
treaties bind all states, including those that have refused to sign or ratify them
questions.explanation: Article 26 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties states that every treaty in force is binding on its parties and must be performed in good faith. A treaty binds only its parties, and withdrawal generally follows the treaty's own terms.

questions.stem: A state agrees to be bound by a multilateral treaty but excludes one article that conflicts with its domestic laws. What has the state made?
options: An advisory opinion
A reservation
An accession
A declaration of war
questions.explanation: A reservation is a statement by which a state excludes or modifies the legal effect of certain provisions in their application to it. It is not allowed if it is incompatible with the treaty's object and purpose. Accession is a way of joining a treaty a state did not sign.

questions.stem: Australia ratifies an international treaty. Why does the treaty not, by itself, change the rights of people in Australian courts?
options: Treaties apply in Australia only after the High Court has approved them in a special treaty hearing
Treaties bind only the states and territories, so the Commonwealth cannot rely on them in its courts
Treaties apply in Australian courts only after the UN Secretary-General has certified them for Australia
Treaties must be implemented by legislation passed by parliament before they become part of domestic law
questions.explanation: Australia takes a dualist approach: the executive makes treaties, but they create rights and duties in domestic law only when parliament legislates to implement them. Courts may still use ratified treaties to help resolve ambiguity when interpreting a statute.

questions.stem: Which constitutional power allows the Commonwealth Parliament to pass laws implementing treaties that Australia has ratified?
options: The taxation power in section 51(ii)
The external affairs power in section 51(xxix)
The naval and military defence power in section 51(vi)
The trade and commerce power in section 51(i)
questions.explanation: The High Court has held that the external affairs power supports laws that implement Australia's treaty obligations, as in Koowarta v Bjelke-Petersen (1982), which upheld the Racial Discrimination Act 1975. The other heads of power concern defence, interstate and overseas trade, and taxation.

questions.stem: What is the role of the Joint Standing Committee on Treaties in the Commonwealth Parliament?
options: It hears complaints from individuals who claim Australia has breached one of its treaty obligations
It decides which treaties bind the states, and orders state parliaments to pass laws implementing them
It inquires into treaty actions tabled in parliament and reports on whether Australia should take them
It signs treaties on behalf of Australia once the Governor-General has given approval to the treaty
questions.explanation: Since 1996 proposed treaty actions have been tabled in parliament with a National Interest Analysis and reviewed by the Joint Standing Committee on Treaties, which reports and makes recommendations. Treaties are made by the executive, and complaints about breaches go to bodies such as UN treaty committees.

questions.stem: A state refuses to accept the jurisdiction of an international court over a dispute about its borders. Which statement best explains why the court cannot simply hear the case?
options: Because international courts can hear cases only between states that belong to the same intergovernmental organisation
Because of state sovereignty, international courts generally need a state's consent before they can decide a dispute involving it
Because border disputes are matters of domestic law, international courts are banned from hearing them under the UN Charter
Because only the General Assembly may decide border disputes, and it must do so by a two-thirds majority vote of its members
questions.explanation: Sovereign states are not subject to outside courts unless they consent, whether by special agreement, a treaty clause or a declaration accepting jurisdiction. Border disputes are classic international disputes and are often decided by the ICJ when both states consent.

questions.stem: Which example best shows Australia meeting a responsibility it has under international law?
options: Applying a new UN General Assembly declaration in its courts as if it were a binding Commonwealth statute
Refusing to allow any UN body to comment on its laws because comment would breach Australian sovereignty
Treating every treaty it has signed but not ratified as binding domestic law that overrides state laws
Submitting periodic reports to UN treaty bodies on how it is implementing human rights treaties it has ratified
questions.explanation: Ratifying human rights treaties brings obligations to report regularly to the relevant UN committees, and Australia also takes part in the Human Rights Council's Universal Periodic Review. Declarations are not binding statutes, and signed but unratified treaties do not become domestic law.

questions.stem: Which is one of the purposes of the United Nations set out in Article 1 of the UN Charter?
options: To create a single world currency for trade
To elect the governments of all member states
To write the criminal law of each member state
To maintain international peace and security
questions.explanation: Article 1 lists the UN's purposes: maintaining international peace and security, developing friendly relations among nations, achieving international cooperation on economic, social, cultural and humanitarian problems, and promoting respect for human rights. The UN does not elect governments or write domestic laws.

questions.stem: Which organ of the United Nations includes every member state, each with one vote?
options: The General Assembly
The Security Council
The Secretariat
The International Court of Justice
questions.explanation: Every UN member state has a seat and one vote in the General Assembly. The Security Council has 15 members, the Secretariat is the UN's staff headed by the Secretary-General, and the ICJ is a court of 15 judges.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly matches a principal organ of the United Nations with its role?
options: The Trusteeship Council has primary responsibility for international peace and security
The International Court of Justice manages the day-to-day administration of the UN
The Economic and Social Council coordinates the UN's economic, social and related work
The Secretariat decides disputes between states and gives advisory opinions to the UN
questions.explanation: ECOSOC coordinates economic, social and environmental work and consults with NGOs. The ICJ decides disputes and gives advisory opinions, the Security Council has primary responsibility for peace and security, and the Secretariat runs the UN's daily work.

questions.stem: How does the United Nations participate in the development of international law?
options: It provides a forum where states negotiate and adopt treaties, such as the major human rights covenants
It passes laws through the General Assembly that bind every member state's citizens directly
It appoints the judges of each member state's highest court to ensure they apply international law
It enforces treaties by sending the Secretariat's police force into any state that breaches them
questions.explanation: Many treaties have been negotiated and adopted through the UN, such as the ICCPR and ICESCR of 1966, and the International Law Commission helps codify international law. The General Assembly cannot make laws that bind citizens directly, and the UN has no police force to enforce treaties.

questions.stem: What is an intergovernmental organisation (IGO)?
options: An organisation of private citizens that campaigns on global and international issues
A company that trades in several countries and is owned by shareholders
A domestic government department that manages a state's foreign affairs
An organisation whose members are states, created by agreement between them
questions.explanation: IGOs, such as the UN, the World Trade Organization and ASEAN, are formed by treaties between states, which are their members. Groups of private citizens that campaign internationally, such as Amnesty International, are non-government organisations.

questions.stem: How does the World Trade Organization encourage cooperation among nation-states?
options: It tries business leaders accused of crimes against humanity committed during trade disputes
It controls each member's currency and sets interest rates for all of its member states
It provides agreed trade rules and a system for settling trade disputes between member states
It sets the minimum wage for workers in every member state that trades with any other member
questions.explanation: The WTO administers trade agreements and has a dispute settlement system that members use instead of trade wars. It does not set wages, conduct criminal trials or control currencies; interest rates are set by each state's central bank.

questions.stem: In Whaling in the Antarctic (2014), Australia took Japan to the International Court of Justice. What does the case show about the court?
options: It gives advisory opinions only, so its finding in the case was a recommendation that bound neither state
It resolves disputes between states, and found Japan's whaling program was not for purposes of scientific research
It tries individuals for crimes, and convicted the captains of Japanese whaling ships of breaching marine law
It hears appeals from the High Court of Australia on any question about Australia's international obligations
questions.explanation: The ICJ found that Japan's JARPA II program was not for purposes of scientific research under the whaling convention and ordered that permits under it be revoked. It decides disputes between consenting states; it does not try individuals or hear appeals from national courts.

questions.stem: Which statement about the International Court of Justice is correct?
options: It has nine judges appointed for life and sits at UN headquarters in New York
It has five judges, one from each permanent member of the Security Council
It has 193 judges, one appointed by each member state of the United Nations
It has 15 judges elected for nine-year terms and sits in The Hague
questions.explanation: The ICJ has 15 judges elected by the General Assembly and the Security Council for nine-year terms, and it sits at the Peace Palace in The Hague. There is no rule giving the permanent members a judge each.

questions.stem: Which international court or tribunal would most likely hear a dispute between two states about the interpretation of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea?
options: The UN Human Rights Committee in Geneva
The High Court of Australia in Canberra
The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea
The International Criminal Court in The Hague
questions.explanation: The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, based in Hamburg, was set up under the Convention to decide disputes about it; states may also choose the ICJ or arbitration. The ICC tries individuals, and the Human Rights Committee monitors the ICCPR.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of an NGO participating in international law?
options: The World Trade Organization settling a dispute between two member states about import tariffs
Australia's parliament passing a law to implement a convention that Australia has ratified
Amnesty International publishing reports on human rights abuses and lobbying states to ratify treaties
The Security Council imposing an arms embargo on a state that has invaded one of its neighbours
questions.explanation: NGOs are independent of government; they investigate, report, lobby and campaign, and some have consultative status with ECOSOC. The Security Council and WTO are intergovernmental bodies, and a parliament is part of the state.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the role of NGOs in international law?
options: They are more effective than states, because they can order sanctions against states that break treaties
They raise awareness and influence states, but they cannot make or enforce binding international law themselves
They are the main source of binding international law, because their reports become treaties once published
They have no influence on international law, because only states may attend meetings at the United Nations
questions.explanation: NGOs such as Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch shape agendas and can push for new treaties, but only states make treaties and only bodies such as the Security Council can impose sanctions. Some NGOs take part in UN processes through consultative status.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the relationship between rights and responsibilities?
options: Rights exist only when a person has first carried out all their responsibilities
Exercising a right usually brings a responsibility to respect the rights of others
A person who has a right is free of all responsibilities while using that right
Responsibilities apply only to governments, while rights apply only to individuals
questions.explanation: Rights and responsibilities go together: the right to freedom of expression, for example, comes with a responsibility not to defame others or incite violence. Individuals as well as governments have responsibilities, and most rights are not conditional on first meeting duties.

questions.stem: Which is an express right in the Australian Constitution?
options: Freedom from arbitrary arrest by police in section 128
Trial by jury for indictable Commonwealth offences in section 80
Freedom of speech on all subjects for all Australians in section 51
The right to vote in state elections in section 109
questions.explanation: Section 80 provides that the trial on indictment of any offence against Commonwealth law shall be by jury. The Constitution has no general free speech right, section 109 deals with inconsistent laws, and section 128 sets out how the Constitution is changed.

questions.stem: Section 92 of the Constitution provides that trade, commerce and intercourse among the states shall be absolutely free. What does this protect?
options: Every business from any law that regulates trade, such as safety standards or licensing rules
The right of every Australian to buy goods from overseas without paying any customs duty
The right of state governments to tax goods made in other states at a higher rate than local goods
Interstate trade and movement from laws that discriminate to protect one state's local producers
questions.explanation: The High Court has held that section 92 strikes down laws that burden interstate trade in a discriminatory, protectionist way, while general regulation is allowed. Customs duties are a separate matter under section 90, and taxing other states' goods more heavily would breach section 92.

questions.stem: In Lange v Australian Broadcasting Corporation (1997), the High Court confirmed the implied freedom of political communication. Which statement about this freedom is correct?
options: It allows a person to sue anyone who stops them speaking, including private employers and media companies
It was added to the Constitution by referendum, so only another referendum could remove the freedom
It limits the law-making power of parliaments rather than giving individuals a personal right to free speech
It is written in section 116 of the Constitution and protects all forms of speech on any subject at all times
questions.explanation: The implied freedom arises from the system of representative and responsible government in the Constitution. It operates as a restriction on legislative and executive power, and a law burdening political communication may still be valid if it is reasonably appropriate and adapted to a legitimate end. Section 116 concerns religion.

questions.stem: A cafe in Newcastle refuses to serve a customer because of her race. Which laws give her rights that may have been breached?
options: The Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth) and Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW)
The Crimes Act 1900 (NSW) and the Migration Act 1958 (Cth)
The Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) and the Local Government Act 1993 (NSW)
The Australian Constitution, sections 116 and 117, and the Marriage Act 1961 (Cth)
questions.explanation: Both the Commonwealth Racial Discrimination Act and the NSW Anti-Discrimination Act make race discrimination in providing goods and services unlawful. The Fair Work Act deals with employment, and sections 116 and 117 of the Constitution concern religion and discrimination based on state residence.

questions.stem: Which is a strength of statute law as a source of rights, compared with constitutional rights?
options: Statutory rights bind every country, because Australian statutes apply under international law as well
Parliament can create detailed rights for specific areas and update them as society's values change
Statutory rights can never be removed by parliament, because they are entrenched once they are passed
Statutory rights are made by judges, so they can be developed case by case without parliament's input
questions.explanation: Parliament can legislate detailed protections, such as discrimination laws, and amend them as needed. The same flexibility is a weakness: a later parliament can repeal or limit the rights, unlike constitutional rights, which need a referendum to change.

questions.stem: Which right has its origins in the common law rather than in the Constitution or a statute?
options: Freedom of religion in section 116
Just terms for acquired property
Protection from state residence discrimination
The presumption of innocence
questions.explanation: The presumption of innocence developed through judge-made law and is a fundamental principle of the criminal justice system. Freedom of religion, just terms for acquisition of property and protection from discrimination based on state residence are express constitutional provisions.

questions.stem: Under the principle of legality, how do courts approach a statute that might take away a fundamental common law right?
options: They declare the statute invalid, because a parliament has no power to change any common law right
They apply the statute only to people who have consented in writing to give up the common law right
They refer the statute to the UN Human Rights Committee for a binding ruling on whether it is valid
They presume parliament did not intend to remove the right unless it used clear and unambiguous words
questions.explanation: Courts interpret statutes on the presumption that parliament does not intend to abrogate fundamental rights without clear words. Parliament can still override the common law if it does so clearly; for example, NSW legislation in 2013 allowed unfavourable inferences from silence in some serious cases after a special caution.

questions.stem: In Toonen v Australia (1994), the UN Human Rights Committee found that Tasmanian laws breached the right to privacy in the ICCPR. What happened next, and what does it show?
options: The Commonwealth passed a law protecting sexual privacy, showing international views can prompt domestic change
The High Court enforced the committee's ruling directly, showing that ratified treaties are automatically domestic law
The committee fined Tasmania for the breach, showing that UN committees can impose binding penalties on states
The ICC prosecuted Tasmanian officials, showing that human rights breaches are treated as international crimes
questions.explanation: The committee's views are not binding, but the Commonwealth responded with the Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act 1994, relying on the external affairs power. The case shows international protection working through political pressure and domestic legislation, not through direct enforcement.

questions.stem: A person in NSW believes she has suffered unlawful discrimination under the Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW). Where would her complaint usually go first?
options: Anti-Discrimination NSW, which tries to resolve it by conciliation
The NSW Court of Criminal Appeal, which hears it as a criminal case
The High Court of Australia, which hears all discrimination claims
The International Court of Justice, which hears individual claims
questions.explanation: Complaints under the NSW Act are made to Anti-Discrimination NSW, which investigates and tries conciliation; unresolved complaints may be referred to the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal. The ICJ hears only disputes between states, and discrimination is generally a civil matter rather than a criminal one.

questions.stem: Which is a likely consequence when a tribunal finds that a business has breached a person's right not to be discriminated against?
options: A prison sentence for the business owner, imposed by a magistrate after a jury trial
An order from the UN Security Council requiring the business to close permanently
Automatic loss of the owner's citizenship and removal of the business from the state
An order to pay damages or to take steps such as apologising or changing a policy
questions.explanation: Discrimination is generally a civil wrong, so remedies are compensatory and corrective, such as damages, apologies or changes to practices. Imprisonment follows criminal convictions, and the Security Council deals with threats to international peace, not individual complaints.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates international protection of rights for a person in Australia?
options: It is unavailable, because Australia has not ratified any international treaties that protect human rights
It replaces domestic protection, because a person must take any rights complaint to the UN before a court
It can expose breaches and pressure governments, but UN committee views cannot be enforced in Australian courts
It is fully effective, because UN committee decisions bind Australian courts in the same way as statutes do
questions.explanation: Australia has ratified major treaties and allows individual complaints under some of them, but committee views are recommendations that depend on government willingness to act. Domestic remedies must normally be exhausted first, and they remain the main avenue for enforcing rights.
